content: Bronchodilators are frequently administered to treat acute bronchiolitis in children, although their effectiveness remains uncertain. This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of epinephrine in children under two years of age diagnosed with acute viral bronchiolitis. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, Scopus, PubMed, LILACS, and Iran MedEx, covering studies published up to September 2010. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials that compared epinephrine to either a placebo or another intervention in children under two years of age with acute viral bronchiolitis. Only studies reporting at least one quantitative outcome of interest were included. The primary outcomes were pre-defined and included the rate of hospital admission by Day 1 and Day 7 for outpatients, as well as the length of hospital stay (LOS) for inpatients. Secondary outcomes included clinical severity scores, pulmonary function, symptom resolution, quality of life, and adverse events. Two independent reviewers screened the studies, applied the inclusion criteria, assessed the risk of bias, and graded the quality of evidence. Separate analyses were performed based on the comparison groups (placebo, non-epinephrine bronchodilators, glucocorticoids) and the clinical setting (inpatient versus outpatient). A total of 19 studies involving 2,256 participants were included in the analysis. Among outpatients, epinephrine demonstrated a significant reduction in hospital admission rates on Day 1 compared to placebo (risk ratio [RR] 0.67; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.50 to 0.89). However, this benefit was not observed at Day 7 following the emergency department visit. For inpatients, there was no significant difference in the length of hospital stay when comparing epinephrine to placebo. When epinephrine was compared to salbutamol, no differences were observed in admission rates for outpatients on either Day 1 or Day 7. However, inpatients treated with epinephrine had a significantly shorter length of hospital stay compared to those receiving salbutamol (mean difference -0.28 days; 95% CI -0.46 to -0.09). Additionally, one large randomized controlled trial found that a combination of epinephrine and steroids significantly reduced the admission rate at Day 7 compared to placebo (RR 0.65; 95% CI 0.44 to 0.95). Importantly, no significant differences in adverse events were reported across the studies. The authors concluded that epinephrine is superior to placebo for short-term outcomes in outpatients, particularly within the first 24 hours of care. Preliminary evidence from a single study suggests that combining epinephrine with steroids may provide additional benefits at later time points. However, further research is needed to confirm the efficacy of this combination in outpatient settings. There is currently no evidence supporting the effectiveness of repeated doses or prolonged use of epinephrine, either alone or in combination with dexamethasone, for inpatients.
